title: The brave new world of psychedelic therapies for mental health - Dr Sarah McKay
abstract:
## Regulatory approval of psychedelic drugs in Australia  
Australia is now the first country in the world to approve psychedelics as a medicinal treatment.  
But there are currently no approved medicines that contain either MDMA or psilocybin in Australia. That means authorised psychiatrists currently will need to source unapproved medicine that contains these substances for patients.  
There have also been some reservations about prescription psychedelics, with some clinicians believing the move is premature.  
Nevertheless, the announcement has provided new hope to individuals with mental health disorders who haven’t responded to treatment. About one in three people with depression don’t respond to standard pharmaceutical and psychological treatments.
## Potential uses in the clinic beyond psychiatry  
In tandem with rising cases of mental health disorders, neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease are also increasing globally with an ageing population. Scientists have started to investigate how the [plasticity-promoting potential](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jnc.15544) of psychedelics could protect the brain, increase new neurons or potentially rewire connections to slow or even prevent cognitive decline.  
Harnessing psychedelics’ [regenerative effects](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0014488620300765) has led to the investigation of whether psychedelics can heal brain damage from [stroke](https://psychedelicspotlight.com/prolonged-dmt-infusions-could-be-a-breakthrough-for-stroke-patients/).
## The future of psychedelic drugs  
The development of psychedelic drugs may usher in the next generation of psychiatry and neurology treatments.  
Clinical trials with psychedelics so far have been encouraging, but as of yet psychedelic therapy has not reached medical approval. Psychedelic trials are [difficult to run](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34038314/), particularly as those enrolled have high expectations that could bias reported effectiveness.  
But the elephant in the room that could limit people’s willingness to use psychedelics is their very nature as hallucinogens. Although many rate psychedelic trips as some of the most [meaningful experience](https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/eco.2022.0044)s of their lives, there is still a stigma associated with psychedelic use.  
Could taking the trip out of psychedelic drugs still retain their therapeutic effectiveness?  
Initial [studies with mice](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7874389/) suggest yes, and these “non-hallucinogenic psychedelics” might open doors to new therapy programs and further increase their acceptance.  
About the author.  
*Dr Amy Reichelt is a passionate psychedelic drug development professional. She serves as a board member at the Women in Psychedelics Network and holds a PhD in Neuroscience (Cardiff University), and is recognized as a leader in cognitive neuroscience, nutrition neurobiology and behavioural pharmacology.*
